warmup.q: A merchant profile is cached in Redis with EX 3600 and read 100 times a second by one pod. Loading it from the database takes 200 ms. The key expires. With plain cache-aside (GET, on a miss load and SET), about how many database queries does that pod send for this one row?
options: 1: the first miss reloads it and the rest hit
About 20: one per request that arrives during the 200 ms load
100 or more if the requests arrive together: every one that misses before the reload finishes queries the database
0: Redis reloads expired keys from the database itself
warmup.why: Nothing tells the other requests that a load is already running, so every request that misses before the first SET lands queries the database too. With requests arriving together, that is all of them: in the lesson's demo 100 concurrent misses made 100 calls. At a steady 100 a second it would be about 20, one per request during the 200 ms. Redis never loads anything by itself; in cache-aside your code does.

sections.h: Cache-aside: ask Redis first, load from the database on a miss
sections.html:
The fraud check on every card authorization needs the merchant's profile: name, country and merchant category code. The profile lives in an Oracle table, and the query costs about 120 ms with its round trip. At 2,000 authorizations a second that is 2,000 queries a second, for rows that change maybe once a month.

A cache keeps a copy of hot rows somewhere faster. The simplest version is a HashMap inside each pod. It breaks once you run 20 pods: each pod loads every merchant for itself, so the database still sees 20 loads per merchant, and when a merchant changes there are 20 copies to fix and no way to reach them. A shared Redis fixes both. There is one copy, and every pod reaches it in well under a millisecond.

The usual way to use it is cache-aside, also called lazy loading. Your application does all the work:

  1. GET merchant:m-17. If Redis has it, that is a hit: decode it and return.
  2. On a miss, load the row from the database.
  3. SET merchant:m-17 <row> EX 3600, so the next reader finds it, and return.

Redis never talks to Oracle. It holds whatever your code put there, for as long as the TTL allows (lesson 4).

What you gain is an average. With hits at 0.3 ms and misses at 120 ms, a 95% hit ratio (the share of reads that are hits) gives 0.95 × 0.3 + 0.05 × 120 = 6.3 ms on average, and 99% gives 1.5 ms. Near the top, every point of hit ratio is worth a lot, so everything that causes misses matters: cold starts, evictions, and TTLs that are too short.

The TTL is your staleness budget. A merchant renamed in the database keeps its old name in the cache until the key expires or your code deletes it. An hour is fine for a display name. It is not fine for a card's blocked flag. Pick each TTL by asking how long a wrong answer may live.

Two other patterns move loading out of your code. With read-through, a cache library loads on a miss for you; Caffeine's LoadingCache works this way inside one JVM. With write-through, every write goes to the cache and the database together. Write-behind writes the cache first and the database later, and loses those writes if the cache dies in between. For payments, use cache-aside and keep the database the one source of truth.

try.title: Time a miss and three hits
steps: Start the lab server if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d from the labs folder).
Run CacheAsideDemo (Java) or CacheAsideDemoKt (Kotlin). Its "database" sleeps 120 ms per query. Predict the four timings before you run it.
Run it a second time without deleting anything first. What changes, and why? (The demo deletes the key at the start, so look closely.)

code.title: CacheAsideDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.redis.l05.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams; /** Cache-aside in front of a "database" that takes 120 ms: one miss, then hits. */ public class CacheAsideDemo { static int dbCalls = 0; // the system of record: in production an Oracle query behind a connection pool static String loadFromDatabase(String id) throws InterruptedException { dbCalls++; Thread.sleep(120); return id + "|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940"; } static String getMerchant(RedisClient redis, String id) throws InterruptedException { String key = "merchant:" + id; String cached = redis.get(key); // 1. ask Redis first if (cached != null) return cached; String row = loadFromDatabase(id); // 2. a miss: go to the database redis.set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); // 3. keep it for an hour return row; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del("merchant:m-17"); redis.get("warm-up"); // open a pooled connection first for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String row = getMerchant(redis, "m-17"); System.out.printf("read %d: %-30s %7.2f ms (database calls so far: %d)%n", i, row, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6, dbCalls); } System.out.println("TTL merchant:m-17 = " + redis.ttl("merchant:m-17") + " s"); } } }

alt.title: CacheAsideDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.redis.l05.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams /** Cache-aside in front of a "database" that takes 120 ms: one miss, then hits. */ private var dbCalls = 0 // the system of record: in production an Oracle query behind a connection pool private fun loadFromDatabase(id: String): String { dbCalls++ Thread.sleep(120) return "$id|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940" } private fun RedisClient.getMerchant(id: String): String { val key = "merchant:$id" get(key)?.let { return it } // 1. ask Redis first val row = loadFromDatabase(id) // 2. a miss: go to the database set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) // 3. keep it for an hour return row } fun main() { RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { redis -> redis.del("merchant:m-17") redis.get("warm-up") // open a pooled connection first for (i in 1..4) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val row = redis.getMerchant("m-17") println("read %d: %-30s %7.2f ms (database calls so far: %d)".format(i, row, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6, dbCalls)) } println("TTL merchant:m-17 = ${redis.ttl("merchant:m-17")} s") } }

try.expect: The first read is a miss at about 125 ms (read 1: m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940 127.73 ms (database calls so far: 1)). Reads 2 to 4 are hits at well under a millisecond to about 2 ms; the first hit is often the slowest while the JIT warms up. The database count stays at 1, and TTL merchant:m-17 = 3600 s. A second run looks the same, because the demo deletes the key first: every fresh JVM starts with one miss. Your numbers depend on your laptop and on Docker.

sections.h: Writes make the cache wrong: delete the key after the commit
sections.html:
Cache-aside has a weakness built in: the database changes and Redis doesn't know. Rename a merchant, and Oracle has the new name while merchant:m-17 keeps the old one for up to an hour.

The first fix most people reach for is to update the cache on every write: after UPDATE merchants ..., also SET merchant:m-17 <new row>. That works with one writer and breaks with two. Writer A renames the merchant to "Fietsen A", and writer B, a moment later, to "Fietsen B". The database ends with B, because B committed last. But the two SETs travel to Redis on their own, and if A's arrives after B's, the cache says "Fietsen A" while the database says "Fietsen B". Nothing corrects it until the TTL runs out.

So delete instead. After the database commit, DEL merchant:m-17. A delete carries no value, so two deletes in either order leave the same thing, an empty slot, and the next reader loads the fresh row. Delete after the commit, never before. Delete first, and a reader that misses in between reloads the old row and caches it again.

One race is left, and the simulator below lets you play it. A reader misses and reads the old row from the database. Before its SET arrives, a writer commits the new row and deletes the key, which is already empty. Then the reader's SET puts the old row back. It needs a slow reader and a write inside a window of a few milliseconds, so it is rare. When it happens, the TTL caps how long the wrong row can live. That cap is the reason every cache entry gets a TTL, even the ones you invalidate.

When even a short wrong answer is unacceptable, don't cache that data, or cache it for seconds. A card's blocked flag belongs in the authorization's own database read, not behind an hour of cache.

sim.title: A reader puts an old row back
sim.intro: cache = 0 means no key; the numbers are row versions. The writer commits version 2 and deletes the key. Can you end with the cache holding version 1?

goal.say: Stale: the database has version 2, and the cache will serve version 1 until its TTL ends. The reader read before the commit and wrote after the delete.

sections.h: Keys that expire together, and lookups for things that don't exist
sections.html:
Two load patterns hurt cache-aside even when the code is right.

The first is keys that expire together. A deploy warms the cache by loading 50,000 merchant profiles in one minute, all with EX 3600. An hour later they all expire within the same minute, and that minute's traffic misses on every one of them: 50,000 extra queries for Oracle on top of the normal load, while lesson 4's active expiry deletes 50,000 keys on Redis's single thread. Then they are all reloaded in the same minute again, and the spike comes back every hour.

The fix is jitter: a random spread on each TTL. With 3600 × (1 ± 0.1), the same 50,000 keys expire across 12 minutes instead of one, about 4,200 a minute instead of 50,000. Each reload gets a new random TTL, so the spread holds after that. It costs one line, and some entries live 6 minutes longer than the nominal hour, which is fine for data you already accepted as an hour stale.

The second pattern is lookups for things that don't exist. A partner's integration keeps sending authorizations for merchant ids that were never created, or a scraper walks ids. Each lookup misses in Redis, finds nothing in Oracle, and caches nothing, because there was nothing to cache. Every one goes to the database, every time. This is called cache penetration.

The fix is negative caching: cache the "not found" as well. Store a marker that can't be a real row, such as <missing>, with a short TTL, 60 seconds instead of an hour. Keep it short, because a merchant created a minute later should show up without waiting an hour. Your read path now has three cases to tell apart. Nil from Redis means "not cached, go and look". The marker means "known to be missing, return null". Anything else is a row.

The lab's MerchantCache does both: rows get a jittered TTL, and missing ids get a 60-second marker.

try.title: See jitter spread the deadlines
steps: At the redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), paste the first two commands. They write 10,000 keys with exactly 3,600 seconds, and 10,000 more with 3,600 seconds plus or minus 10%.
The next two EVALs count, for each key family, how many keys expire in each minute from now. Predict both answers first.
Run the last four commands: a negative entry for a merchant that doesn't exist. Which GET tells you "known missing" and which "never looked"?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
EVAL "for i = 1, 10000 do redis.call('SET', 'flat:' .. i, 'x', 'EX', 3600) end return 1" 0
EVAL "for i = 1, 10000 do redis.call('SET', 'jit:' .. i, 'x', 'EX', math.floor(3600 * (0.9 + 0.2 * math.random()))) end return 1" 0
EVAL "local h = {} for i = 1, 10000 do local m = math.floor(redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1] .. i) / 60) h[m] = (h[m] or 0) + 1 end local out = {} for m in pairs(h) do table.insert(out, m) end table.sort(out) for i, m in ipairs(out) do out[i] = 'minute ' .. m .. ': ' .. h[m] end return out" 1 flat:
EVAL "local h = {} for i = 1, 10000 do local m = math.floor(redis.call('TTL', KEYS[1] .. i) / 60) h[m] = (h[m] or 0) + 1 end local out = {} for m in pairs(h) do table.insert(out, m) end table.sort(out) for i, m in ipairs(out) do out[i] = 'minute ' .. m .. ': ' .. h[m] end return out" 1 jit:
SET merchant:m-404 "<missing>" EX 60
GET merchant:m-404
TTL merchant:m-404
GET merchant:m-405

try.expect: The flat family answers with a single line, 1) "minute 60: 10000" (or minute 59 if a second ticked over): every key dies in the same minute. The jittered family spreads over 12 lines, from minute 54 to minute 65, with roughly 800 to 880 keys each. Then SET prints OK, GET merchant:m-404 returns "<missing>" (known missing: return null and skip the database), TTL is (integer) 60, and GET merchant:m-405 returns (nil) (nothing cached: go to the database). math.random gives different numbers on every run, so your jittered counts will differ a little from these.

sections.h: A stampede: a hundred requests miss the same key at once
sections.html:
Jitter spreads different keys apart. It can't help with one hot key. merchant:m-17 is the busiest merchant on a sale day, read 100 times a second in each pod. When its TTL ends, the next requests all miss before any of them has put the row back, because loading takes 200 ms. Every one of them goes to the database for the same row. In the lesson's demo, 100 concurrent misses made 100 database calls. Oracle runs one query 100 times, a connection pool of 20 queues the rest, and every other query in the service waits behind them. This is a cache stampede, also called a thundering herd.

The fix inside one JVM is single-flight: let the first miss load, and make the others wait for its result. A ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Merchant>> is enough. The first thread whose putIfAbsent succeeds becomes the leader and queries the database. The others get the leader's future back and join() it. When the load ends, the leader completes the future, every waiter wakes with the same value, and the leader removes the entry, so the next miss starts a fresh load. Caffeine's Cache.get(key, loader) and Guava's LoadingCache coalesce loads the same way. In the demo, single-flight took 100 database calls down to 1, and everyone waited about 210 ms, one query's time.

Single-flight only reaches threads in the same JVM. In the demo, 4 pods made 4 calls, so 20 pods would make 20. To get to one across pods, the pods agree through Redis. The pod that wins SET lock:merchant:m-17 <token> NX PX 2000 (NX: only if the key doesn't exist; PX: expire in 2,000 ms) loads the row. The others poll the cache every 10 ms for up to a second, then give up and load it themselves. The demo made 1 call across 4 pods. This lock only saves work: if it fails, two pods load the same row, which is harmless. Lesson 8 is about locks that must never fail.

The last option avoids the miss altogether: refresh a hot key before it expires. A reader that finds the key close to its deadline reloads it in the background while everyone keeps reading the old value. Go deeper shows XFetch, a version where each reader decides at random, with odds that rise as the deadline nears.

All 99 followers wake up with the same value, and the leader removes the map entry, so a later miss starts a fresh load. frames.say: Single-flight works inside one JVM. Twenty pods each have their own map, so the database still gets 20 queries. To get to one, the pods coordinate through Redis: the pod that wins SET lock:merchant:m-17 <token> NX PX 2000 loads the row, and the others poll the cache for a moment. In the demo, 4 pods made 4 calls with single-flight and 1 with the lock.

try.title: Count the database calls in a stampede
steps: Run StampedeDemo (Java) or StampedeDemoKt (Kotlin). It releases 100 requests at once on a cold key four times: with no protection, with single-flight in 1 pod, with single-flight in 4 pods (25 requests each), and with a Redis lock across the 4 pods.
Predict the database calls for each line, and whether the lock makes anyone wait longer.
Read redisLock(). What happens to the waiting pods if the lock holder crashes before its SET?

code.title: StampedeDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.redis.l05.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams; import redis.clients.jedis.util.CompareCondition; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.UUID; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 100 requests miss the same cold key at once. How many reach the 200 ms database? */ public class StampedeDemo { static final String KEY = "merchant:m-17"; static final AtomicInteger dbCalls = new AtomicInteger(); static String loadFromDatabase() { dbCalls.incrementAndGet(); sleep(200); return "m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940"; } /** One service instance: its own Redis client and its own in-process single-flight map. */ static final class Pod { final RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build(); final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> flights = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String plain() { // cache-aside, no protection String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; v = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); return v; } String singleFlight() { // one load per key per pod String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; CompletableFuture<String> mine = new CompletableFuture<>(); CompletableFuture<String> running = flights.putIfAbsent(KEY, mine); if (running != null) return running.join(); // a follower waits for the leader try { String row = redis.get(KEY); // filled while we became leader? if (row == null) { row = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); } mine.complete(row); return row; } finally { flights.remove(KEY, mine); } } String redisLock() { // one load per key across all pods String v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); if (redis.set("lock:" + KEY, token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null) { try { v = loadFromDatabase(); redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)); return v; } finally { // Redis 8.4+: delete the lock only if it is still ours (lesson 8 explains why) redis.delex("lock:" + KEY, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)); } } for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { // someone else is loading: wait for the cache sleep(10); v = redis.get(KEY); if (v != null) return v; } return loadFromDatabase(); // waited a second: load it ourselves } } interface Strategy { String get(Pod pod); } static void run(String label, int pods, Strategy strategy) throws Exception { List<Pod> fleet = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < pods; i++) fleet.add(new Pod()); fleet.get(0).redis.del(KEY, "lock:" + KEY); dbCalls.set(0); ExecutorService threads = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100); CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1); List<CompletableFuture<String>> requests = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Pod pod = fleet.get(i % pods); requests.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { await(start); return strategy.get(pod); }, threads)); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); start.countDown(); requests.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); System.out.printf("%-40s database calls: %3d %4d ms%n", label, dbCalls.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); threads.shutdown(); fleet.forEach(p -> p.redis.close()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run("no protection, 1 pod", 1, Pod::plain); run("single-flight, 1 pod", 1, Pod::singleFlight); run("single-flight, 4 pods", 4, Pod::singleFlight); run("Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods", 4, Pod::redisLock); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } static void await(CountDownLatch latch) { try { latch.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } }

alt.title: StampedeDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.redis.l05.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.params.SetParams import redis.clients.jedis.util.CompareCondition import java.util.UUID import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** 100 requests miss the same cold key at once. How many reach the 200 ms database? */ private const val KEY = "merchant:m-17" private val dbCalls = AtomicInteger() private fun loadFromDatabase(): String { dbCalls.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(200) return "m-17|Fietsen Utrecht|NL|5940" } /** One service instance: its own Redis client and its own in-process single-flight map. */ private class Pod { val redis: RedisClient = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build() private val flights = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>>() fun plain(): String { // cache-aside, no protection redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val v = loadFromDatabase() redis.set(KEY, v, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) return v } fun singleFlight(): String { // one load per key per pod redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val mine = CompletableFuture<String>() flights.putIfAbsent(KEY, mine)?.let { return it.join() } // a follower waits for the leader try { val row = redis.get(KEY) ?: loadFromDatabase().also { // filled while we became leader? redis.set(KEY, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) } mine.complete(row) return row } finally { flights.remove(KEY, mine) } } fun redisLock(): String { // one load per key across all pods redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() if (redis.set("lock:$KEY", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null) { try { return loadFromDatabase().also { redis.set(KEY, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(3_600)) } } finally { // Redis 8.4+: delete the lock only if it is still ours (lesson 8 explains why) redis.delex("lock:$KEY", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) } } repeat(100) { // someone else is loading: wait for the cache Thread.sleep(10) redis.get(KEY)?.let { return it } } return loadFromDatabase() // waited a second: load it ourselves } } private fun run(label: String, pods: Int, strategy: (Pod) -> String) { val fleet = List(pods) { Pod() } fleet[0].redis.del(KEY, "lock:$KEY") dbCalls.set(0) val threads = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100) val start = CountDownLatch(1) val requests = (0 until 100).map { i -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ start.await(); strategy(fleet[i % pods]) }, threads) } val t0 = System.nanoTime() start.countDown() requests.forEach { it.join() } println("%-40s database calls: %3d %4d ms".format(label, dbCalls.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) threads.shutdown() fleet.forEach { it.redis.close() } } fun main() { run("no protection, 1 pod", 1, Pod::plain) run("single-flight, 1 pod", 1, Pod::singleFlight) run("single-flight, 4 pods", 4, Pod::singleFlight) run("Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods", 4, Pod::redisLock) }

try.expect: no protection, 1 pod prints database calls: 100, single-flight, 1 pod prints 1, single-flight, 4 pods prints 4, and Redis lock (SET NX PX), 4 pods prints 1. Every line takes about 205 to 245 ms: one query's time, because all 100 requests wait in parallel. The lock costs a little more, because the losers poll every 10 ms. Here the fake database never slows down under load; a real one with 100 identical queries and a pool of 20 would make the first line much slower. If the lock holder crashes, the lock expires after 2,000 ms, and the waiters give up after about a second and load the row themselves. delex with CompareCondition.valueEq needs Redis 8.4 or newer.

refs.title: SET (NX, PX and the 8.4 IFEQ condition)

analogy: Cache-aside is the bread shelf by a bakery's door. Customers take a loaf from the shelf; when it is empty, a customer walks to the back and asks the baker to bake one, which takes a while. The shelf has a sell-by sticker (the TTL), and when the baker changes the recipe, someone has to clear the old loaves off the shelf rather than slip new ones next to them. A stampede is the shelf going empty at 9:00 with a hundred customers in the shop, all walking to the back at once. Single-flight is the first customer telling the others "I've asked, wait here". The analogy breaks on visibility: in a shop everyone sees the queue at the baker, but your pods see nothing of each other, which is why they need a sign on a shared board, the Redis lock.
world: Card-issuer BIN tables, merchant profiles, FX rates, fraud-model feature flags and partner configuration are all read on the authorization path and change rarely. They are good cache-aside candidates, each with its own TTL chosen by how long a wrong answer may live. Anything that decides money (a card's blocked flag, an account's available balance) is not. If a Quarkus service already uses an in-process cache such as Caffeine, keep it: it coalesces concurrent loads inside the pod, and the shared Redis layer behind it is what stops 20 pods from loading the same row 20 times. Watch keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses from INFO stats next to your database's query rate. A miss spike at the same minute every hour is synchronized TTLs, and the fix is one line of jitter.
mistake: The most common mistake is updating the cache on write with SET instead of deleting it, and leaving out the TTL because "we always update it". Two writers whose SETs arrive at Redis in the opposite order from their commits leave the wrong row in the cache, and with no TTL it stays wrong until someone notices and flushes it by hand. It happens because updating feels more efficient than deleting: the next reader doesn't have to load. The fix is to commit to the database, then DEL the key, and give every cache entry a TTL as the upper bound on how long any remaining race can leave it wrong.

compare.title: Cache-aside with a negative marker, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: MerchantCache.java
java.html: public Merchant get(String id) { String cached = redis.get("merchant:" + id); if (cached != null) { // a hit: a row or the marker return MISSING.equals(cached) ? null : Merchant.decode(cached); } Merchant m = repository.find(id); // a miss: the slow part if (m == null) { redis.set("merchant:" + id, MISSING, SetParams.setParams().ex(60)); } else { redis.set("merchant:" + id, m.encode(), SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))); } return m; }

kotlin.title: MerchantCache.kt
kotlin.html: fun get(id: String): Merchant? { redis.get("merchant:$id")?.let { cached -> // a hit: a row or the marker return if (cached == MISSING) null else Merchant.decode(cached) } val m: Merchant? = repository.find(id) // a miss: the slow part if (m == null) { redis.set("merchant:$id", MISSING, SetParams.setParams().ex(60)) } else { redis.set("merchant:$id", m.encode(), SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))) } return m }

compare.note: The Redis traffic is identical: one GET, and on a miss one SET with a TTL that depends on what the database said. Kotlin's ?.let { return ... } turns the hit into an early return, and its nullable types make the three outcomes visible: redis.get returns String? (not cached), MISSING maps to a null Merchant? (known missing), and anything else decodes. Java gets the same result with explicit null checks. Neither version handles the stampede yet; the lab adds single-flight in front of the repository call.

worked.title: Stop a stampede across pods with a Redis lock

steps.say: Start from the hit. Only a miss needs coordination. On a miss, try to become the one pod that loads: SET lock:<key> <token> NX PX 2000 succeeds for exactly one caller, because SET NX runs to completion on Redis's single thread (lesson 1). The token is a random value that says whose lock it is.
steps.code: String v = redis.get(key); if (v != null) return v; String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); boolean leader = redis.set("lock:" + key, token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null;

alt.html: redis.get(key)?.let { return it } val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() val leader = redis.set("lock:$key", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(2_000)) != null

steps.say: The leader loads and fills the cache, then releases the lock. Release only your own lock: if the load took longer than 2 seconds, the lock has expired and may belong to another pod by now. Redis 8.4's DELEX ... IFEQ deletes only if the value still matches; before 8.4 this needs a small Lua script (lesson 8).
steps.code: if (leader) { try { String row = loadFromDatabase(key); redis.set(key, row, SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))); return row; } finally { redis.delex("lock:" + key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)); } }

alt.html: if (leader) { try { return loadFromDatabase(key).also { redis.set(key, it, SetParams.setParams().ex(jitteredTtl(3_600, 0.1, random))) } } finally { redis.delex("lock:$key", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) } }

steps.say: Everyone else waits for the cache, briefly. Poll every 10 ms for up to a second. If the leader died, stop waiting and load it yourself: a second load is wasted work, not a wrong answer.
steps.code: for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Thread.sleep(10); String row = redis.get(key); if (row != null) return row; } return loadFromDatabase(key); // the leader is gone or slow: load anyway

alt.html: repeat(100) { Thread.sleep(10) redis.get(key)?.let { return it } } return loadFromDatabase(key) // the leader is gone or slow: load anyway

steps.say: Measure it. In the lesson's demo, 4 pods with 25 concurrent requests each made 4 database calls with per-pod single-flight and 1 with the lock, at about the same latency. Combine the two in production: single-flight first, so only one thread per pod even tries for the lock.

lab.title: Single-flight, then a cache-aside cache with jitter and negative entries
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 15 fail: six in SingleFlightTest and two in JitteredTtlTest need no Docker, and seven in MerchantCacheTest use the shared Redis container. The repository in the tests is a fake that sleeps and counts its calls.

In SingleFlight.kt, write load. The KDoc gives the three steps: claim with putIfAbsent, follow by joining, lead by loading and completing. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.redis.l05.SingleFlightTest' until its six tests pass.
Write get: GET, decode a hit (the marker means null), and on a miss go through flights.load(id, () -> ...). Inside the loader, GET once more, then ask the repository and SET with the right TTL.
Run all 15 tests. Read a hundred concurrent misses for one merchant reach the repository once: it is the stepper's frame 5, with a real Redis.
hints: flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) returns null when you claimed the key. Kotlin's ?: gives a compact shape: val running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) ?: return lead(...).
join() wraps the leader's exception in a CompletionException. Catch it and throw e.cause ?: e, so followers see the same IllegalStateException as the leader.
Remove the entry in a finally with flights.remove(key, mine), the two-argument form: it removes only your own future.
In Java, flights.load(id, () -> { ... return m; }) works because a Kotlin () -> V is a Function0<V>, which a Java lambda can implement.

drill.title: Single-flight from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write load(key, loader) for a single-flight with a ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<V>>: one loader call per key at a time, followers get the leader's value or its exception, and the entry disappears when the load ends. Then compare. Which line makes sure only one caller leads?

answer.html: fun load(key: String, loader: () -> V): V { val mine = CompletableFuture<V>() val running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine) // atomic: exactly one caller gets null if (running != null) { try { return running.join() } catch (e: CompletionException) { throw e.cause ?: e } } try { return loader().also { mine.complete(it) } } catch (e: Throwable) { mine.completeExceptionally(e) throw e } finally { flights.remove(key, mine) // not a cache: the next miss loads again } }

alt.html: V load(String key, Supplier<V> loader) { CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>(); CompletableFuture<V> running = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine); // atomic: exactly one caller gets null if (running != null) { try { return running.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { throw e.getCause() instanceof RuntimeException r ? r : e; } } try { V value = loader.get(); mine.complete(value); return value; } catch (RuntimeException e) { mine.completeExceptionally(e); throw e; } finally { flights.remove(key, mine); // not a cache: the next miss loads again } }

recap: Cache-aside: GET from Redis; on a miss, load from the database and SET with a TTL. Redis never talks to the database.
The TTL is the staleness budget, and it caps every invalidation race. Give every cache entry one.
On a write, commit to the database, then DEL the key. Updating the cache with SET loses races between writers.
Jitter TTLs (for example 3,600 s ± 10%) so keys loaded together don't expire together; cache "not found" with a short TTL.
A hot key's expiry is a stampede. Single-flight collapses the misses inside one JVM; a SET NX PX lock in Redis does it across pods.

explain.prompt: The DBA asks why Oracle's query rate for the merchants table spikes to 40 times normal at 10 past every hour, and lasts about a minute. The service caches merchants in Redis with EX 3600, warmed by a job at deploy time. Explain what is happening and what you will change.
explain.answer: The warm-up job loaded every merchant within about a minute, all with exactly 3,600 seconds of TTL, so they all expire within the same minute an hour later. During that minute every read of every merchant is a miss and goes to Oracle, the rows are reloaded with exactly 3,600 seconds again, and the spike repeats every hour. Hot merchants make it worse: when one expires, every concurrent request for it misses before the first reload finishes, so the same row is queried dozens of times at once. I'll add jitter, for example 3,600 seconds plus or minus 10%, so the expiries spread over 12 minutes and stay spread. And I'll put single-flight in front of the database call so each pod loads a given merchant once, with a short Redis lock for the few hottest merchants so only one pod loads them.

deeper.html:
XFetch (Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein, VLDB 2015) refreshes a hot key before it expires, without any lock. Store, next to the value, how long the last load took (delta). On every read, recompute early if

now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry

rand() is uniform in (0, 1], so -ln(rand()) is a positive random number, usually around 1 and rarely much larger. Far from the deadline the condition almost never holds. In the last few multiples of delta before it, the odds climb fast, so one reader usually refreshes the key a little early while the rest keep reading the old value. beta (1 by default) makes refreshes earlier and stampedes rarer. The paper shows that this exponential choice is optimal and needs no tuning for the request rate.

Client-side caching moves the cache into your JVM and lets Redis tell you when to drop an entry. With RESP3, a connection can turn on tracking: Redis remembers which keys that client read and sends an invalidation message on the same connection when one of them changes, expires or is evicted. Jedis 8 builds this in with .cacheConfig(CacheConfig.builder().maxSize(1000).build()) on a RESP3 client. A hit then costs no network trip at all. The price is server memory for the tracking table (or prefix-based broadcasting instead), and a short window after a write in which other clients' local copies are still old.

Serve-stale is the simplest stampede fix of all for data that tolerates it: keep a second, longer-lived copy (or a soft deadline inside the value), answer with the old row while one loader refreshes it, and never let readers wait.

sources.title: Jedis: connect, including client-side caching (Redis docs)
